# Hexagonal Grids

Hex geometry lives in `src/app/grid/hexGeometry.ts` and rendering in `src/app/grid/hexGridDrawer.ts`.

- **Size convention**: `grid.size` is the flat-to-flat distance of a hex (width of a pointy-top hex, height of a flat-top hex), the same convention Foundry VTT and Owlbear Rodeo use. Circumradius is `size / sqrt(3)`. A size-1 token therefore has the same pixel diameter on hex and square grids.
- **Orientation**: `hex-vertical` = pointy-top (rows), `hex-horizontal` = flat-top (columns).
- **Coordinates**: axial `(q, r)` with cube rounding for pixel-to-hex (Red Blob Games). Never round `q` and `r` independently.
- **Origin**: `(offsetX, offsetY)` is the top-left of hex `(0, 0)`'s bounding box, so a hex map whose first hex is flush with the image corner aligns at offset 0.
- **Drawing**: each row/column emits one zig-zag polyline plus one straight edge per hex, so every edge is drawn exactly once (no edge deduplication, no double-drawn lines). The `Graphics` is drawn in world space and clipped by a map-sized mask; do not bake it into a texture (that introduced sub-pixel offsets in the past).
- **Distance**: hex steps via `axialDistance`; square grids use Chebyshev distance. The ruler and the drag ruler measure with `pathLengthInCells` (`grid/gridDistance.ts`), which prices a square grid's diagonals by the collection's `DiagonalRule`. Never count cells from a pixel distance as it comes: snapped points lie whole cells apart, but the division by the cell size misses the whole number by a rounding error that depends on the place, so `cellsBetween` takes a distance within a millionth of a cell of whole cells as whole. A token with an even footprint snaps to where cells meet, on a hex grid a vertex that lies in no one hex, so the drag ruler measures between the cells the footprint starts from (`DragRuler.cellPath`, the snapped centre less `tokenCenterShift`).
- **Dotted style**: vertex markers are single filled polygons (`drawVertexMarker`), never overlapping strokes, so the centre stays crisp at any opacity. The `GridSystem` fills for dotted and strokes otherwise.
- **Linked hexes**: a `NotePin` with `hex: true` links its note to the hex containing its point (`grid/hexLinks.ts`), so a realigned grid keeps it on the same part of the map; on non-hex grids it falls back to a pin. At rest it shows only its pin, which `PinRenderer` draws in the centre of the hex (`pinDisplayPoint`) but never hit-tests. `HexLinkRenderer` draws the hover, press and Shift-preview highlight (DM-only, above the lighting, `MAP_LAYER_Z.hexLinks`) and `HexLinkInteraction` handles hover, click-to-open (the press stays unhandled so drags still pan) and the context menu, dispatched from `TokenRenderer` for the select and move tools. The Note Pin tool links with Shift (`tools/notePinPreview.ts`); a hex holds one note.
- **Alignment**: the panel has a grid type of its own (the scene's to begin with; auto-detect sets it), and a measurement alone never changes the GM's choice. On hex grids each measurement is two corners of one hex. Meant is one edge, but people click the corners "left and right" of a hex, which read as an edge of the other orientation gave huge hexes of the wrong type: `hexAlignmentCandidates` (`hexAlignmentMath.ts`) works out every reading (an edge, opposite corners, corners with one between them, whose hex lies to either side), the chosen type before the other orientation, seeds the lattice from the first pair and fuses further pairs with a beam search over lattice-vertex assignments plus least squares. Two pairs along one axis are inherently scale-ambiguous; a third in another direction resolves it. A measurement or a freehand placement is then fitted to the map's lines (`snapGridToMapGray`, `useGridFit`; the panel's switch turns it off): the candidates only name a type and a rough size, the detector's lattice fit places the grid, its stretch included, and of sizes that are multiples of each other the densest wins as in detection. So one measurement is enough where the map has lines (the Intersections tab asks after the first and once more after the fourth), and the four measurements are the fallback where it has none. Clicked points are world points of the map as it was stretched then (`mapStretch` on the candidates). Applying is one undo step (`runHistoryTransaction` around the store's `alignGrid` and the token re-snap). What was measured belongs to the map it was measured on: the panel ends itself when its view loads another scene, and a detection that answers after the GM went on (Reset, a tab, a grid type) is dropped. Scene thumbnails wait while the panel is open (`SceneThumbnailUpdater`), since the canvas shows the preview and the panel's marks.
- **Map stretch** (`GridState.mapStretch`, `grid/mapStretch.ts`, read with `readMapStretch`): many maps are printed with cells that are not regular (hexes a few percent too tall, squares that are rectangles), and scans lie a fraction of a degree askew. `MapStretch` carries both: `x` / `y` and `rotation` (degrees the image lies turned, at most `MAX_ROTATION_DEGREES`); `MosaicCanvas` turns the tile layer level about the image's centre in an inner container and stretches the box that then holds it (`turnedBox`), whose corner is the world's origin, so `worldRect` is that box. The grid stays regular; the map image is drawn stretched along one axis so that its cells are, as Foundry and Roll20 do, and only ever grows (`stretchForAspect`), so it keeps every pixel. The stretch is part of the alignment: size and offsets are in the stretched world, `gridAlignedTo` writes them together, one undo step. `MosaicCanvas.setStretch` scales its layer and reports the stretched `worldRect` (`imageSize` is the image's own size); views and demand regions are brought back into image pixels there, so the tile layer never knows. A load shows the image with its file's stretch and `MapController.followStretch` follows the store outside loads. The alignment panel previews a stretch on the map itself (`GridAlignmentController.showPreview`); cancelling puts the store's back. What stands on the map keeps its place on the image when an applied alignment draws the map another way: `alignGrid(grid, move)` writes the grid and every object moved by `movedWithMap` (`objectsMovedWithMap`, `grid/mapStretchObjects.ts`: tokens, pins, texts, lights, audio, drawings, walls, zones, fog; sizes stay) in one write, so walls stay on the map's walls and a token in its hex, and undo takes both back. Anything new that has a place on the map goes into `objectsMovedWithMap`. The explored memory is no object: its texture is fitted to the map's new size, which is exact for a stretch and a little off for a turn. A preview is the map image and the grid alone: while the image is drawn another way than the store's grid says (`isPreviewingStretch`), the fog, the lighting and the explored memory keep the scene's size, so a cancelled preview changes nothing (the players' picture is pixel-identical after it) and a lit scene's preview shows the light where the scene has it; `mapSizeSettled` lets them follow once the store's stretch is the image's (a load, an applied alignment and its undo, through `followStretch`'s `onFollowed`). The renderer fits the zoom range again to the map's new size (`fitZoomRangeToStretch`). A fit whose aspect no stretch in range makes regular (`MAX_STRETCH_FACTOR`) found no grid. The grid is clipped to the image, which of a turned map is its `outline` and not the world rect's empty corners. `tests/gpu/mosaicCanvasStretch.gpu.test.ts` draws a stretched map.
- **Auto-detect**: `src/app/pixi/spectralEngine/` works as propose, fit, verify. *Propose*: the power spectrum of the map's line contrast (square = axis peaks, hex = six peaks at 30°+k·60° pointy / k·60° flat) is summed over harmonics, because thin lines are a comb whose fundamental is its weakest peak on textured art; two views propose (contrast before and after downsampling, for thin and thick lines). The spectrum never decides anything. *Fit*: `edgeProfile.ts` averages the image along each cell edge before rectifying, so faint lines add up coherently; `latticeSearch.ts` profiles ~800 edges once and scores every nearby size/offset by reading those profiles (one vote per edge, so heavy ink cannot outvote a faint grid); `latticeFit.ts` then measures each edge's sub-pixel distance to its line and solves size and offset in one robust least-squares (distances are linear in the three unknowns because every grid point is `origin + size * latticeCoordinate`; Tukey weights with a shrinking cutoff drop hidden edges and map art). Edges come from the real drawers via `gridTemplate.ts`, so detection and rendering cannot disagree. *Verify*: `support` is the chance-corrected share of edges with a line within 0.75 px, taken over the weakest edge direction (another grid type can share one direction's lines, never all); below 0.05 the map has no grid and the manual tool is the fallback. Size multiples are compared at equal edge length (longer edges see fainter lines) and the smallest within 75% of the best wins. Size changes scale about the image centre. Mind the half-pixel convention: detected pixel indices get `+0.5` before becoming world coordinates. *Stretched grids*: every candidate has an `aspect` (the image's rows lie that many times further apart than a regular grid's) and lives on the squared-up image, the image with its rows that much closer together (`LatticeCandidate`; `edgeResponse` samples through it, nothing is resampled). To first order the aspect moves every line in proportion to its distance from the centre row, so `fitLattice(..., free)` solves it as a fourth linear unknown. A regular grid is kept unless the lines support another aspect clearly better (`refineGrid`), and an aspect that moves no line by half a pixel is the regular grid. Where the regular proposals settle nothing (no support of 0.5), a second round is fitted (`secondRoundProposals`): regular proposals from line evidence that ignores edges (`lineContrast`: the blocks of a JPEG and painted areas propose nothing) and proposals of other aspects from every view (`stretchedHypotheses`: the same peaks with their vertical frequency divided by the aspect, 1 % steps up to a quarter either way), each view's best of each type before anyone's second best (scores of types and views do not compare), twelve at most, since every map without a grid pays for each. The result names the stretch the map needs (`AlignmentResult.mapStretch`, `gridInWorld`). `detectGridInImage(image, hint)` looks only for a hint's type at about its size, for the alignment panel. *What real maps taught it* (a corpus of about 130 maps): an edge is measured in five pieces and the strongest and weakest never count (`edgeResponse`), since a terrain icon, wall or label across a line is far stronger than the line; the line probe grows with the cell (`lineProbe`) and a wide line is centred by the centre of gravity of its response (`lineCentre`); each proposal is searched where its cells are about 96 px (`SEARCH_CELL_SIZE`, `fitProposal`) and fitted on the image itself (`refineFromReduced`); a scan's angle is a fifth unknown of the fit (`FreeShape`, `LatticeCandidate.rotation`) and is proposed like the aspect (`turnedHypotheses`); small cells of large maps are proposed from windows at the map's middle (`fineProposals`). *Support* counts every edge of the grid, but chance only from the edges that show a line (`edgesOnLines`), so a grid drawn on a dungeon's floors alone counts for what it is. A square grid must also show on long edges (`acceptedSupport`, `LONG_EDGE`): floor boards and tiles look like a grid cell by cell and are on no lattice over 400 px. Of square sizes that are multiples of each other the densest that is no finer copy of the map's grid wins (`isFinerCopy`, `subGrid.ts`: of a finer copy only every second, third or fifth line is ever hit), where counting edges cannot choose on a map that is mostly blank paper; weak fits that are multiples of an accepted one come along. A grid a GM measured needs far less of itself on the lines (`MIN_HINTED_SUPPORT`). *What drawn grids and a review taught it*: a fit that found another shape (aspect, angle) keeps the offsets of the shape it started from and may end beside the lines with the right cells, so the search places it again on the shape it ended with (`reseated`, `refineGrid.ts`; a scan both stretched and askew is found this way). A grid a program drew has harmonics as strong as itself, so a fifth of the cell is proposed first: a spectral peak that turns out a finer copy also proposes three and five times its size (`FINER_COPY_MULTIPLES`, peaks only: on a dungeon whose grid shows on its floors alone, multiples look like finer copies too and theirs took a 634 px lattice for a 49 px grid). Fits supported within `SUPPORT_TIE` of each other are a tie, which the most regular wins. Columns and rows of a square grid fit each on their own, so every fourth line one way and every fifth the other is a "grid" with cells a fifth off regular: unhinted square fits further off than `MAX_DETECTED_SQUARE_ASPECT` are none, and hexes that far off (tile sets draw them) need decisive support. A lattice a few percent off the map's own shares every n-th line with it (`sharesLinesOnly`, `subGrid.ts`: the hits of one direction lie on every n-th line alone): such a square fit never replaces a hint's measurement, and is no grid where detection is left with it. A hint also says which multiple of a spectral peak is meant (`atHintedSizes`). Cells down to `MIN_CELL_SIZE` px of the analysed image are fitted. Known limits: square grids whose cells are rectangles where the spectrum proposes no aspect (found by neither detection nor a hint: the measurement stands as it is), scans whose paper is warped (support near the floor: found on one resampling and not on another), photos taken at an angle, maps made of several panels with a grid each, grids drawn by hand without a ruler, and very small low-quality images.
